variants.question: What is the name of the mental model that involves breaking a large, complicated problem down into smaller, more manageable parts?
What is the name of the mental model that involves imagining how a situation looks from someone else's point of view?
What is the name of the mental model that involves solving a new problem by comparing it to a similar problem you've solved before?
What is the name of the mental model that involves restating a problem in a different way to reveal solutions that weren't obvious at first?

lat_l1_t1.technicalIntricacy: Each mental model offers a different lens for approaching a problem — breaking it apart, viewing it from another angle, borrowing a solution from a similar past problem, or restating it entirely — and skilled problem-solvers often try several of these lenses before settling on an approach.
lat_l1_t1.realPurpose: Having a toolkit of named mental models makes it much easier to deliberately switch strategies when stuck, instead of just repeating the same approach and hoping for a different result.

variants.question: When a student stuck on a maze tries starting from the exit and working backward toward the start, which style of thinking is being used?
distractors: Linear (step-by-step) thinking
Neither lateral nor linear thinking
Both lateral and linear thinking equally

variants.question: When a student solves a maze by simply trying each path one at a time, in order, from the start, which style of thinking is being used?
distractors: Lateral thinking
Neither lateral nor linear thinking
Both lateral and linear thinking equally

variants.question: When a team brainstorms ten different possible solutions before picking the best one, which style of thinking is being used?
distractors: Linear (step-by-step) thinking
Neither lateral nor linear thinking
Both lateral and linear thinking equally

variants.question: When a team picks the very first solution anyone suggests without considering any alternatives, which style of thinking is being used?
distractors: Lateral thinking
Neither lateral nor linear thinking
Both lateral and linear thinking equally

lat_l1_t2.technicalIntricacy: Linear thinking follows a predictable, step-by-step sequence, while lateral thinking deliberately explores unconventional starting points, orders, or perspectives — both are useful, but lateral thinking often uncovers solutions that a strictly linear approach would miss.
lat_l1_t2.realPurpose: Recognising which style of thinking you're using helps you deliberately switch to a lateral approach when a linear one isn't making progress.

variants.question: What is the name of the mental model that involves deliberately imagining the worst possible outcome of a plan in advance, in order to spot and avoid weaknesses before they happen?
What is the name of the mental model that involves working backward from a desired end goal to figure out the steps needed to reach it?
What is the name of the mental model that involves simplifying a complicated problem by removing minor details to focus on its most essential, core structure?

lat_l1_t3.technicalIntricacy: Each of these mental models restructures how a problem is approached — imagining failure in advance, starting from the goal instead of the start, or stripping away non-essential detail — offering a different angle than simply moving forward step by step.
lat_l1_t3.realPurpose: Having several distinct mental models available means a stuck problem-solver has genuine alternatives to try, rather than just repeating the same forward-moving approach.

variants.question: During a brainstorming session, why is it usually best to avoid criticising ideas immediately as they're suggested?
variants.answer: Early criticism discourages people from sharing more unusual or creative ideas that might turn out to be valuable

variants.question: Why can setting a strict time limit sometimes help a brainstorming session produce better ideas?
variants.answer: A time limit encourages quick, unfiltered idea generation rather than overthinking or hesitating on each idea

distractorPool: Criticising ideas immediately always improves the overall quality of a brainstorming session
Time limits are used only to make a session feel more formal, with no effect on the ideas generated
Both practices exist purely as tradition, with no real effect on how many or how creative the resulting ideas are
lat_l1_t4.technicalIntricacy: Effective brainstorming techniques are designed around how people actually think creatively — delaying judgment prevents good ideas from being dismissed too early, and time pressure encourages rapid idea generation instead of premature self-editing.
lat_l1_t4.realPurpose: Understanding why these brainstorming rules work makes it possible to run a genuinely more productive group problem-solving session.

variants.question: What term describes the idea that working within limits or rules can sometimes boost creative thinking rather than restrict it?
What term describes generating as many different ideas as possible before judging or narrowing any of them down?
What term describes narrowing a wide range of ideas down to select the single most promising one?

lat_l1_t5.technicalIntricacy: Divergent thinking widens the pool of possible ideas, convergent thinking narrows that pool down to the strongest option, and constraint-driven creativity shows that limits can actually sharpen creative thinking rather than only restrict it — three distinct forces at work in creative problem-solving.
lat_l1_t5.realPurpose: Recognising these separate phases of the creative process helps a student notice which stage they're in, rather than trying to generate ideas and judge them at the exact same time, which tends to shut creativity down.

variants.question: A student breaks a big science-fair project into smaller tasks — choosing a topic, doing research, building the model, and writing the report — before starting on any of them. Which mental model is being used?
distractors: Perspective-taking
Analogical thinking
Working backward

variants.question: A student tries to complete an entire science-fair project in one single sitting without ever splitting it into smaller tasks, and quickly feels overwhelmed. Which mental model is missing from this approach?
distractors: Perspective-taking
Analogical thinking
Working backward

lat_l1_t6.technicalIntricacy: Decomposition works by turning one large, intimidating task into several smaller, clearly defined ones, each of which is easier to plan, start, and track progress on than the intimidating whole.
lat_l1_t6.realPurpose: Breaking big projects into smaller pieces is one of the most widely used productivity techniques, since it turns a vague, overwhelming goal into a concrete list of manageable next steps.

variants.question: Before proposing a new class rule, a student imagines how a classmate who might dislike the rule would react to it, and adjusts the proposal accordingly. Which mental model is being used?
distractors: Decomposition
Abstraction
Pre-mortem thinking (inversion)

variants.question: A student writes a persuasive essay by only ever considering their own opinion, without imagining how someone who disagrees might respond to their argument. Which mental model is missing from this approach?
distractors: Decomposition
Abstraction
Pre-mortem thinking (inversion)

lat_l1_t7.technicalIntricacy: Perspective-taking means deliberately imagining a situation through someone else's knowledge, priorities and reactions, rather than assuming everyone sees a situation exactly the way you do.
lat_l1_t7.realPurpose: Actively considering other viewpoints leads to proposals, arguments and solutions that hold up better once other people actually react to them, since likely objections have already been anticipated.

variants.question: A student solves a new coding problem by remembering how they solved a similar problem last month, and adapting that same strategy to the new situation. Which mental model is being used?
distractors: Decomposition
Reframing
Working backward

variants.question: A student refuses to consider any problem they've solved before, even when a very similar one comes up again, and insists on starting completely from scratch every single time. Which mental model is being ignored here?
distractors: Decomposition
Reframing
Working backward

lat_l1_t8.technicalIntricacy: Analogical thinking works by identifying the underlying structure shared between a new problem and a previously solved one, then transferring the successful strategy across, even though the surface details of the two problems may look quite different.
lat_l1_t8.realPurpose: Recognising when a new problem resembles one you've already handled saves significant time and effort, instead of reinventing a solution from nothing every time a challenge appears.

variants.question: A student stuck on the question 'How do I get my classmates to stop talking during group work?' restates it as 'How do I make group work interesting enough that no one wants to talk about anything else?' Which mental model is being used?
distractors: Decomposition
Analogical thinking
Abstraction

variants.question: A student stuck on a difficult question keeps repeating the exact same original wording of the problem to themselves over and over, without ever trying to state it differently. Which mental model is missing from this approach?
distractors: Decomposition
Analogical thinking
Abstraction

lat_l1_t9.technicalIntricacy: Reframing works by changing the words or angle used to state a problem, which can shift attention away from an unproductive detail and toward a more solvable version of the same underlying challenge.
lat_l1_t9.realPurpose: Many problems that feel impossible are actually just phrased in an unhelpful way, so restating them is often enough to reveal a solution that was there all along.

variants.question: A student is told a poster design must use no more than two colours and no photographs, and this restriction pushes them to come up with a bold, unusual design they wouldn't have considered otherwise. What does this illustrate?
variants.answer: Constraint-driven creativity — a limit that pushes creative thinking in new directions rather than only restricting it
distractors: Limits always reduce the quality of creative work, with no possible upside
The design would have been better if there had been absolutely no restrictions at all
Constraints only ever apply to art projects, never to any other kind of problem-solving

variants.question: A team is given completely unlimited resources, unlimited time, and no rules at all for a class project, and ends up struggling to even choose a starting direction. What does this illustrate about constraints?
variants.answer: A total absence of constraints can sometimes make creative decisions harder, since limits often help focus and direct creative effort
distractors: Having no constraints at all is always the ideal condition for creative work
Struggling with unlimited options proves the team lacks any creative ability
Constraints are only ever unhelpful and have no realistic benefit in any situation

lat_l1_t10.technicalIntricacy: A total lack of constraints can leave so many directions open that choosing becomes difficult, while a well-chosen limit narrows the space of options enough to focus creative effort productively — this is why designers, writers and engineers sometimes add artificial constraints on purpose.
lat_l1_t10.realPurpose: Understanding that limits can help (not just hinder) creativity changes how a student reacts to a restriction, from feeling purely frustrated to actively using it as a creative tool.

lat_l2_t1.technicalIntricacy: Recognising a pattern means identifying the consistent rule connecting each term to the next — here, each number increases by the same fixed amount — and then applying that same rule one more time to predict what comes next.
lat_l2_t1.realPurpose: Pattern recognition is a foundational lateral and logical thinking skill used everywhere from puzzles and coding to spotting trends in real-world data.

variants.question: {{n}} friends want to split {{total}} stickers equally among themselves. How many stickers will each friend receive?
distractors: {{total}}
{{distractorB}}

lat_l2_t2.technicalIntricacy: Splitting a total amount equally among a group means dividing the total by the number of people, which is a simple but essential building block for fair resource-allocation puzzles.
lat_l2_t2.realPurpose: Fair-sharing logic like this comes up constantly in everyday decisions, from splitting a bill to dividing tasks evenly among a team.

variants.question: A student has {{shirts}} different shirts and {{pants}} different pairs of pants. How many different shirt-and-pants outfit combinations can they make, pairing any shirt with any pair of pants?
distractors: {{distractorA}}
{{distractorB}}
{{distractorC}}

lat_l2_t3.technicalIntricacy: When choosing one item from each of two independent groups, the total number of possible combinations is found by multiplying the size of each group together, since every item in one group can be paired with every item in the other.
lat_l2_t3.realPurpose: This basic combinatorial counting principle underlies far more complex logic puzzles, probability problems, and even password-strength calculations.

variants.question: Look at this number pattern: {{start}}, {{seq2}}, {{seq3}}, {{seq4}}, ___. What number comes next?
distractors: {{distractorA}}
{{distractorC}}

lat_l2_t4.technicalIntricacy: In this pattern, each number is found by multiplying the previous one by the same fixed factor, rather than adding a fixed amount — recognising a multiplying (geometric) pattern rather than an adding (arithmetic) one is key to predicting the next term correctly.
lat_l2_t4.realPurpose: Distinguishing between additive and multiplicative patterns is essential in mathematics and appears in real growth patterns, from compound interest to population growth.

variants.question: A student is assigned a research project on a topic they know nothing about, with no similar past project to copy from and only a few days before the deadline. Which combination of mental models would most likely help them make quick, effective progress?
variants.answer: Decomposition (splitting the project into smaller steps) combined with working backward from the deadline to build a realistic schedule
distractors: Waiting until closer to the deadline, since more useful information will naturally appear on its own
Relying only on analogical thinking, since an unfamiliar topic guarantees a similar past project must exist somewhere
Skipping any planning and starting immediately without ever splitting the work into smaller steps

variants.question: A team's brainstorming session for a new class poster produces exactly one idea in the first thirty seconds, and everyone immediately agrees to use it without discussing any alternatives. What is the most likely risk in this situation?
variants.answer: Committing to the very first idea too quickly risks missing a stronger solution that further brainstorming might have uncovered
distractors: There is no risk at all, since the very first idea generated in any brainstorm is always the strongest one
The risk is that the team spent too much time thinking, since thirty seconds is already far too long for a decision
Group agreement always guarantees an idea is the best possible option, regardless of how quickly it was reached

lat_l2_t5.technicalIntricacy: Combining mental models — like decomposition to break work into steps and working backward from a deadline to sequence them — is often more effective than relying on just one strategy alone, since each model compensates for a different limitation of the others.
lat_l2_t5.realPurpose: Real projects with unfamiliar topics and real deadlines are exactly where combining multiple lateral-thinking strategies pays off most, rather than in simple practice problems where only one strategy is needed.

variants.question: A student is stuck trying to solve a puzzle using only one approach, and keeps getting the same wrong answer. A friend suggests trying to look at the problem 'upside down' or from a completely different angle instead of repeating the same method again. What is the benefit of this advice?
variants.answer: Repeating the exact same approach that already failed rarely produces a different result; deliberately switching to a new mental model or perspective (lateral thinking) increases the chance of noticing a detail or approach the original method was blind to
distractors: The friend's advice is unhelpful — sticking with the exact same method and trying it more times is always the fastest way to eventually succeed
Switching approaches should only ever be considered after at least twenty failed attempts with the original method
Looking at a problem differently is only useful for art and creative subjects, not for logic puzzles

lat_l3_t1.technicalIntricacy: When a specific approach isn't working, it often means that approach has a blind spot — some assumption or detail it isn't accounting for; switching to a genuinely different mental model changes which details become visible, often revealing exactly the piece that was missing.
lat_l3_t1.realPurpose: This is why experienced problem-solvers deliberately keep a variety of strategies on hand, rather than relying on a single 'default' method for every situation.

variants.question: A student assumes that because their teacher's suggested method works well for most problems, it must be the only valid method that could possibly work for this new, unusual problem. What is the flaw in this assumption?
variants.answer: Most problems can be approached using more than one valid strategy or mental model; even a generally reliable method might not be the most efficient or effective for every specific situation, so staying open to alternative approaches usually leads to more flexible, creative problem-solving
distractors: The student is correct — once a method is proven reliable for most problems, it is guaranteed to work for absolutely every new problem too
Trying an alternative method to a teacher's suggested approach is never appropriate, even if the original method clearly isn't working
Every problem has exactly one single correct method, and all other approaches are automatically wrong

lat_l3_t2.technicalIntricacy: A method being reliable across many typical problems doesn't guarantee it's optimal (or even applicable) for every unusual edge case; genuinely flexible problem-solving involves recognising when a situation calls for a different tool, rather than forcing every problem through the same familiar process.
lat_l3_t2.realPurpose: This flexible mindset helps students adapt confidently when they encounter unfamiliar problems that don't fit the patterns they've been taught to expect.

variants.question: A student always solves problems by immediately trying to recall a memorised formula, and gets stuck completely on a new problem that doesn't match any formula they've memorised. What is the flaw in this approach?
variants.answer: Relying solely on memorised formulas works only for problems that closely match previously seen patterns; genuinely novel problems often require reasoning from first principles or trying a different mental model altogether, rather than searching for a matching formula that may not exist
distractors: The student is correct — every possible problem can always be solved by recalling the right memorised formula, if the student simply thinks hard enough
Getting stuck like this proves the student needs to memorise even more formulas before attempting any new problem
Novel problems that don't match a memorised formula are, by definition, unsolvable

lat_l3_t3.technicalIntricacy: Memorised formulas are shortcuts derived from deeper underlying reasoning, and they only apply directly to problems shaped like the ones they were derived for; a truly novel problem may require returning to that deeper reasoning (first principles) or applying a different mental model entirely, rather than searching indefinitely for a matching memorised shortcut.
lat_l3_t3.realPurpose: Recognising when memorised formulas run out is what separates flexible problem-solvers from those who can only handle familiar problem types.

variants.question: A student dismisses a classmate's unusual suggested solution immediately, assuming that because it 'sounds strange,' it must be wrong. What is the flaw in this reasoning?
variants.answer: Many genuinely effective creative solutions initially sound unusual or counterintuitive, precisely because they don't follow the most obvious, conventional path; dismissing an idea purely because it sounds strange (without actually evaluating whether it would work) risks discarding a valuable, creative solution before it's ever properly considered
distractors: The student is correct — any solution that sounds unusual or strange can be safely assumed to be incorrect without further evaluation
Unusual-sounding ideas should always be adopted immediately, without any evaluation, simply because they sound different
The strangeness of an idea is always a perfectly reliable measure of whether or not it will actually work

lat_l3_t4.technicalIntricacy: Lateral thinking specifically works by exploring unconventional angles, which means genuinely useful lateral solutions often sound odd at first, precisely because they diverge from the expected, obvious path; the actual test of an idea's value is whether it logically works when examined, not how conventional or familiar it initially sounds.
lat_l3_t4.realPurpose: This is why productive brainstorming and problem-solving requires briefly suspending judgment long enough to properly evaluate unusual ideas before rejecting them.

variants.question: What term describes a situation that is unclear or open to more than one interpretation?
What term describes giving up one benefit in order to gain another when choosing between options?
What is it called when you list the advantages and disadvantages of each option to help compare them?
What term describes the different possible results that could happen after a decision is made?

amb_l1_t1.technicalIntricacy: These terms form the basic vocabulary of thoughtful decision-making: recognising ambiguity, identifying trade-offs, organising a comparison, and anticipating possible outcomes are each distinct steps in reasoning through a complex choice.
amb_l1_t1.realPurpose: Having precise language for these ideas makes it easier to talk through a difficult decision clearly, whether alone or with someone helping you think it through.

variants.question: Which is the most helpful strategy when facing a decision with incomplete information?
variants.answer: Gathering the most important available information, then making a reasonable choice despite some remaining uncertainty
distractors: Waiting indefinitely until every single possible piece of information is known before deciding anything
Choosing whichever option requires the least effort to think about
Flipping a coin, since incomplete information makes any reasoning pointless

variants.question: Which is the most helpful strategy for comparing two very different options fairly?
variants.answer: Listing the specific trade-offs and priorities that matter most for the decision
distractors: Assuming the more expensive or more popular option is automatically the better choice
Choosing based only on which option was suggested first
Avoiding any comparison at all, since the options are too different to compare

variants.question: Which is the most helpful mindset when a well-reasoned decision doesn't lead to the best outcome?
variants.answer: Recognising that some factors were outside anyone's knowledge or control, and learning from the experience
distractors: Assuming a bad outcome always means the decision-making process itself must have been careless
Deciding to never make an important decision independently again
Concluding that careful thinking is generally a waste of time

amb_l1_t2.technicalIntricacy: Good decision-making under uncertainty balances gathering enough information to be reasonably confident against the reality that waiting for perfect certainty is often impossible or too costly in time.
amb_l1_t2.realPurpose: These strategies are used by professionals in every field — from doctors to engineers to business leaders — who regularly have to make sound decisions without having every possible piece of information.

variants.question: What term describes making a judgment based on limited information, using reasonable assumptions to fill the gaps?
What term describes intentionally delaying a decision specifically to gather more relevant information first?
What term describes a decision-making approach that considers several different possible future scenarios before choosing a path?

amb_l1_t3.technicalIntricacy: Each of these strategies manages uncertainty differently — an educated guess fills a gap with reasonable assumptions, deliberate information-gathering reduces the gap before deciding, and scenario planning prepares for several different possible futures at once.
amb_l1_t3.realPurpose: Knowing multiple named strategies for handling uncertainty means a person facing ambiguity has real options, rather than only guessing or freezing indecisively.

variants.question: What term describes choosing a guaranteed smaller benefit over a larger but uncertain one?
What term describes choosing a larger but uncertain potential benefit over a smaller guaranteed one?

distractorPool: A completely random choice, unrelated to risk or benefit
A choice that ignores all potential benefits entirely
A choice that is always objectively the correct one to make
amb_l1_t4.technicalIntricacy: Risk tolerance describes a consistent pattern in how someone weighs a guaranteed smaller outcome against a larger but uncertain one, and reasonable people can have very different risk tolerances without either approach being universally 'correct.'
amb_l1_t4.realPurpose: Understanding your own risk tolerance helps explain why you might make different choices than someone else facing the exact same decision with the exact same information.

variants.question: What term describes preparing a backup plan in case your first choice doesn't work out as expected?
What term describes the benefit you give up from the next-best alternative when you choose one option over another?
What term describes choosing an option that is 'good enough' rather than continuing to search endlessly for the single best possible option?

amb_l1_t5.technicalIntricacy: These three ideas each manage a different part of decision-making under ambiguity: preparing for an unfavourable outcome in advance, recognising what's given up by choosing one option, and knowing when 'good enough' is the sensible stopping point.
amb_l1_t5.realPurpose: Naming these strategies precisely makes it possible to actually use them on purpose during a real decision, rather than only vaguely sensing that a choice involves some kind of trade-off or risk.

variants.question: What term describes relying too heavily on the first piece of information encountered when making a decision, even when it isn't especially relevant?
What term describes continuing to invest in a decision mainly because of what has already been spent, rather than because it's still the best choice going forward?
What term describes paying attention mainly to information that confirms what you already believed, while overlooking information that contradicts it?

amb_l1_t6.technicalIntricacy: Each of these is a common thinking pattern that can quietly distort an otherwise reasonable decision — being overly influenced by an early number, continuing something purely because of past investment, or noticing only the evidence that already matches your expectations.
amb_l1_t6.realPurpose: Recognising these patterns by name is the first step toward catching yourself using them, which leads to clearer, more balanced decisions under uncertainty.

variants.question: A student spends so long searching for the single 'perfect' book for a report that they run out of time to read anything at all. What decision-making lesson does this best illustrate?
variants.answer: Sometimes it's more effective to choose a reasonably good option quickly (satisficing) than to keep searching endlessly for a perfect one
distractors: Searching as long as possible always leads to the best possible outcome, no matter the cost in time
The student should have picked randomly from the very beginning, since thinking about options is never useful
There is no lesson here, since reading any book at all is equally acceptable regardless of the deadline

variants.question: A student keeps attending a club they no longer enjoy, reasoning 'I've already spent six months on it, so I can't quit now.' What decision-making mistake does this illustrate?
variants.answer: The sunk cost fallacy — letting past investment that can't be recovered drive a decision, instead of focusing on what's genuinely best going forward
distractors: The student is reasoning correctly — past time invested should always be the main factor in any future decision
There is no mistake here, since staying in any activity indefinitely is always the responsible choice
The mistake is only that six months wasn't quite long enough to justify staying

variants.question: A student is deciding whether to join a new activity and asks only friends who already love that activity for their opinion, while ignoring anyone who might feel differently. What decision-making mistake does this illustrate?
variants.answer: Confirmation bias — seeking out only opinions that confirm an existing preference, rather than a balanced range of views
distractors: This is the correct approach, since only enthusiastic opinions are ever useful for making a decision
There is no mistake here, since friends' opinions are always completely unbiased no matter who is asked
The mistake is only that the student didn't ask enough enthusiastic friends

amb_l1_t7.technicalIntricacy: Satisficing, the sunk cost fallacy, and confirmation bias each shape a decision in a different way — settling for 'good enough,' being swayed by unrecoverable past investment, or unconsciously filtering out inconvenient information — and recognising them in a real scenario is more useful than only knowing their dictionary definitions.
amb_l1_t7.realPurpose: Spotting these patterns in everyday situations, like choosing a book, a club, or gathering opinions, builds the practical skill of catching these mistakes in your own decisions before they lead you astray.

variants.question: A student planning an outdoor birthday party also books an indoor backup venue in case it rains. What decision-making strategy is being demonstrated?
distractors: Satisficing
Anchoring (anchoring bias)
The sunk cost fallacy

variants.question: A student plans a single outdoor party with absolutely no backup option, and has no idea what they would do if it rained on the day. What is missing from this plan?
variants.answer: A contingency plan for handling an unfavourable outcome
distractors: Satisficing
Anchoring (anchoring bias)
The sunk cost fallacy

amb_l1_t8.technicalIntricacy: A contingency plan doesn't try to predict exactly what will happen; instead, it prepares a reasonable response in advance for one of the ways things could go wrong, which reduces stress and wasted time if that scenario actually occurs.
amb_l1_t8.realPurpose: Preparing a backup plan is one of the simplest, most practical ways to make a decision more resilient to genuine uncertainty, without needing to know exactly what the future holds.

variants.question: A student can only choose one after-school activity: chess club or art club. By choosing chess club, what have they given up?
variants.answer: The opportunity cost of choosing chess club — the benefit they would have gained from art club instead
distractors: Nothing at all, since choosing one option never involves giving up anything else
The entire value of both clubs combined, since choosing either one cancels out all benefit
Only the membership fee, since opportunity cost refers exclusively to money

variants.question: A student assumes that choosing one option means literally nothing is given up, as long as the chosen option itself turns out well. What is the flaw in this thinking?
variants.answer: Choosing one option, even a good one, still means giving up whatever benefit the next-best alternative would have provided; that giving-up is the opportunity cost, and it exists regardless of how well the chosen option turns out
distractors: The student is correct — a good outcome from the chosen option always means nothing was ever given up
Opportunity cost only applies when the chosen option turns out badly
Opportunity cost is not a real consideration in any decision involving only two options

amb_l1_t9.technicalIntricacy: Opportunity cost isn't about money lost directly; it's about the value of the next-best alternative that becomes unavailable the moment you commit to a different choice, and it applies even when the option you picked turns out to be a good one.
amb_l1_t9.realPurpose: Thinking in terms of opportunity cost helps make trade-offs explicit, which leads to more honest comparisons between options instead of only evaluating the chosen option in isolation.

variants.question: A shop first displays a very high original price for a jacket, then reveals a 'discounted' price that is still more than the student intended to spend, yet it now feels like a great bargain. What decision-making effect is happening here?
variants.answer: Anchoring — the initial high price shifted the student's sense of what counts as a reasonable price
distractors: Satisficing — the student is settling for a good enough price rather than seeking the best one
The sunk cost fallacy — the student has already spent money and cannot back out now
Contingency planning — the student prepared a backup plan in case the price changed

variants.question: In a group discussion, the very first opinion someone shares ends up strongly shaping how the whole group judges every opinion suggested afterward, even ones with equally strong reasoning. What decision-making effect is happening here?
variants.answer: Anchoring — the first opinion shared became a reference point that influenced how later opinions were judged
distractors: Satisficing — the group settled for whichever opinion required the least discussion
The sunk cost fallacy — the group felt they had already invested too much time to consider new opinions
Contingency planning — the group prepared an alternative opinion in case the first one failed

amb_l1_t10.technicalIntricacy: Anchoring happens because the first number or opinion encountered becomes an unconscious reference point, and every option considered afterward tends to be judged relative to that starting point rather than on its own independent merits.
amb_l1_t10.realPurpose: Recognising anchoring helps you evaluate prices, opinions and options more independently, rather than being unknowingly swayed by whatever happened to be presented first.

variants.question: A student is comparing two clubs to join. Club A scores {{scoreA1}} out of 10 for "fun" and {{scoreA2}} out of 10 for "skill-building." Club B scores {{scoreB1}} out of 10 for "fun" and {{scoreB2}} out of 10 for "skill-building." If both factors are weighted equally, which club has the higher total score?
variants.answer: {{winner}}, with a total score of {{winnerTotal}} (compared to the other club's {{loserTotal}})
distractors: {{otherClub}}, with a total score of {{loserTotal}} (compared to the other club's {{winnerTotal}})
Both clubs are tied with equal total scores
Neither club can be compared without more information

amb_l2_t1.technicalIntricacy: When comparing options across multiple factors weighted equally, adding up the scores for each option gives a simple, fair way to compare them directly, even though real decisions often involve weighting some factors more heavily than others.
amb_l2_t1.realPurpose: This kind of simple scoring method is a practical way to organise a decision that initially feels complicated, by turning vague impressions into a clearer, comparable format.

variants.question: A student is deciding whether to bring an umbrella. The weather forecast says there is a {{percent}}% chance of rain. Out of {{trials}} similar days with this same forecast, approximately how many would you expect to actually have rain?
distractors: {{distractorA}}
{{percent}}
{{distractorC}}

amb_l2_t2.technicalIntricacy: A percentage chance describes how often an outcome is expected to happen across many similar situations, so multiplying the percentage by the number of trials estimates how many of those situations would actually see that outcome.
amb_l2_t2.realPurpose: Understanding probability this way helps turn a vague-sounding forecast into a concrete expectation, making it easier to decide reasonably despite genuine uncertainty about any single day.

variants.question: A student refuses to make any decision at all until they have 100% certainty about the outcome, and as a result misses the deadline for both options they were considering. What is the flaw in this approach?
variants.answer: Waiting for complete certainty is often unrealistic, since many real decisions must be made with some remaining uncertainty; refusing to decide is itself a decision (often the worst one, since it can forfeit every option), so learning to act reasonably despite incomplete information is an important skill
distractors: The student made the right call — it is always better to miss every opportunity than to decide with any uncertainty remaining
The mistake was only in choosing the wrong deadline, not in the decision to wait for full certainty
There is no flaw here — total certainty is usually achievable if a person simply waits long enough

amb_l3_t1.technicalIntricacy: Complete certainty about the future is rarely available for any meaningful decision, since it would require knowing every relevant factor in advance; treating 'not deciding' as a safe, neutral choice ignores that it actually forecloses every option once a deadline passes.
amb_l3_t1.realPurpose: Recognising this helps build the confidence to make reasonable, well-considered decisions under realistic conditions, rather than becoming stuck (a pattern sometimes called 'analysis paralysis').

variants.question: After making a well-reasoned decision that didn't turn out well, a student concludes that 'careful decision-making is pointless since things can go wrong anyway.' What is the flaw in this reasoning?
variants.answer: Even a well-reasoned decision can have a disappointing outcome due to factors outside anyone's control, but that doesn't mean the decision-making process was flawed; careful reasoning consistently improves the ODDS of good outcomes over many decisions, even if any single decision can still turn out poorly by chance
distractors: The student is correct — since the outcome was disappointing, the decision-making process must have been careless or flawed
Careful decision-making only matters for decisions that are guaranteed to work out well in advance
The only way to guarantee a good outcome is to avoid making decisions altogether

amb_l3_t2.technicalIntricacy: Decision quality and outcome quality are related but not identical: a good decision-making process accounts for the information available at the time and reasonably weighs the likely outcomes, while the actual result can still be influenced by chance or unknown factors beyond anyone's control.
amb_l3_t2.realPurpose: Separating 'good decision' from 'good outcome' helps people keep making thoughtful choices consistently, rather than abandoning careful reasoning after a single unlucky result.

variants.question: A game offers a reward of {{reward}} points with a {{probability}}% chance of winning. What is the expected value of playing this game (Reward × Probability of winning)?
distractors: {{reward}}
{{distractorB}}
{{distractorC}}

amb_l2_t3.technicalIntricacy: Expected value combines a potential reward with its likelihood into a single number, calculated by multiplying the reward by the probability of winning (expressed as a decimal fraction), giving a useful average outcome if the game were played many times.
amb_l2_t3.realPurpose: Expected value is used to compare different uncertain options fairly, from evaluating simple games of chance to making informed real-world financial and business decisions.

amb_l2_t4.questionTemplate: An option costs {{cost}} points to choose but offers an expected benefit of {{benefit}} points. What is the benefit-to-cost ratio for this option (Benefit ÷ Cost)?
amb_l2_t4.technicalIntricacy: A benefit-to-cost ratio is found by dividing the expected benefit by the cost, giving a single number that shows how much benefit is gained per unit of cost spent — a higher ratio generally indicates a more efficient option.
amb_l2_t4.realPurpose: Benefit-to-cost ratios are used throughout economics, business and public policy to compare very different options on a single, consistent efficiency scale.

variants.question: A student choosing between two summer camps lists the pros and cons of each, asks a few specific questions to fill in missing details, and prepares a backup plan in case their first-choice camp is full. Which combination of strategies for handling ambiguity is being used here?
variants.answer: Organising a pros-and-cons comparison, gathering targeted information to reduce uncertainty, and preparing a contingency plan
distractors: Relying purely on random guessing, since no amount of comparison or information can ever reduce genuine uncertainty
Waiting indefinitely for complete certainty before making any decision at all
Choosing based only on which camp was mentioned first, without any comparison or further information

variants.question: A student facing a decision with several unknowns refuses to gather any further information, refuses to compare pros and cons, and refuses to prepare any backup plan, insisting on simply 'going with their gut' for a choice that will meaningfully affect their year. What is the main risk of skipping every one of these strategies?
variants.answer: Skipping structured information-gathering, comparison and contingency planning increases the chance of overlooking an important trade-off or being unprepared if the decision doesn't work out
distractors: There is no real risk, since gut instinct is always at least as reliable as careful comparison for any decision
The only risk is wasting time, since skipping these strategies always leads to a faster (and equally good) decision
The risk applies only to small, unimportant decisions, never to ones that meaningfully affect a person's year

amb_l2_t5.technicalIntricacy: Real ambiguous decisions are rarely resolved by a single trick; combining several strategies at once — comparing trade-offs, gathering the most relevant missing information, and preparing for an unfavourable outcome — covers more of what can go wrong than relying on just one strategy alone.
amb_l2_t5.realPurpose: Recognising when several ambiguity-navigating strategies are being used together (or skipped together) helps a student evaluate whether a real decision-making process was actually thorough, rather than just checking off one single step.

variants.question: A student refuses to ever take any risk, no matter how small the downside or how large the potential benefit, always choosing 'the safest option' by default. What is the flaw in this approach?
variants.answer: Reasonable decision-making means weighing the actual size of the potential risk against the actual size of the potential benefit case-by-case, not applying a blanket 'never take any risk' rule; sometimes a very small, well-understood risk is clearly worth taking for a much larger potential benefit
distractors: The student is correct — the truly safest strategy in every situation, without exception, is to always avoid any risk whatsoever
Risk should always be accepted, regardless of its size, if there is any potential benefit at all
The size of a potential benefit is completely irrelevant when any risk, however small, is involved

amb_l3_t3.technicalIntricacy: Good decision-making weighs the actual magnitude of a risk against the actual magnitude of a potential benefit in each specific situation; a blanket rule of always avoiding any risk ignores cases where the downside is genuinely tiny or easily recoverable, while the potential upside is substantial, meaning the 'safe' choice can sometimes be the less sensible one.
amb_l3_t3.realPurpose: This case-by-case evaluation is exactly how experienced decision-makers in business, medicine and everyday life choose when a risk is clearly worth taking.

variants.question: After one instance where taking a risk paid off well, a student decides that taking risks always leads to good outcomes, and begins taking increasingly large risks without carefully weighing trade-offs. What is the flaw in this reasoning?
variants.answer: One successful risky outcome doesn't prove that taking risks always pays off — it may have simply been a matter of luck in that specific case; sound decision-making requires evaluating each situation's actual likely trade-offs and probabilities every time, rather than assuming a pattern based on a single previous result
distractors: The student is correct — once a risky choice pays off one time, taking similarly large risks will reliably keep paying off in the future
The single successful outcome proves the student has developed a special skill at correctly predicting risky outcomes
Past outcomes, whether good or bad, should always be completely ignored when making any future decision

amb_l3_t4.technicalIntricacy: A single successful outcome from a risky decision doesn't change the actual underlying probability of success for future, different decisions; treating one lucky result as proof of a reliable pattern (rather than re-evaluating each new situation's specific risks and rewards) is a reasoning error that can lead to increasingly poor decisions over time.
amb_l3_t4.realPurpose: Recognising the difference between a good decision-making process and a lucky one-time outcome is essential for making consistently sound choices, rather than being misled by a single result.

variants.question: What is the belief that abilities can be developed through effort and practice, rather than being fixed traits, called?
What term describes making repeated small improvements over multiple attempts rather than expecting perfection on the first try?
What term describes the useful mental effort of working through a genuinely challenging problem?
What is it called when you specifically examine what went wrong (and why) after a setback, in order to improve?

res_l1_t1.technicalIntricacy: These terms describe the internal skills behind resilience: believing ability can grow, expecting to improve gradually rather than instantly, embracing challenge as useful effort, and deliberately learning from setbacks rather than just feeling upset by them.
res_l1_t1.realPurpose: Having clear names for these ideas makes it easier to notice and practice them deliberately, rather than only experiencing resilience as a vague feeling of 'toughing it out.'

variants.question: After a setback, carefully reviewing which specific steps didn't work, and trying a slightly different approach next time. What type of response is this?
distractors: An unhelpful, fixed-mindset response
Neither a helpful nor an unhelpful response — it has no effect either way
A response that is only helpful for sports, not academic subjects

variants.question: After a setback, deciding never to attempt the task again because the first attempt didn't succeed. What type of response is this?
distractors: A constructive, growth-oriented response
Neither a helpful nor an unhelpful response — it has no effect either way
A response that is only helpful for sports, not academic subjects

variants.question: After a setback, treating a mistake as useful information about what to adjust, rather than as proof of a lack of ability. What type of response is this?
distractors: An unhelpful, fixed-mindset response
Neither a helpful nor an unhelpful response — it has no effect either way
A response that is only helpful for sports, not academic subjects

variants.question: After a setback, assuming that needing more than one attempt at something proves you're simply 'not good' at it. What type of response is this?
distractors: A constructive, growth-oriented response
Neither a helpful nor an unhelpful response — it has no effect either way
A response that is only helpful for sports, not academic subjects

res_l1_t2.technicalIntricacy: A growth-oriented response treats a setback as specific, useful feedback to adjust future attempts, while a fixed-mindset response treats it as final proof of a permanent limitation — the difference in how someone interprets the same event can lead to very different outcomes over time.
res_l1_t2.realPurpose: Learning to recognise these response patterns in yourself makes it easier to deliberately choose the constructive response, even when the unhelpful one feels more automatic in the moment.

variants.question: What term describes bouncing back and adapting well after a difficult setback or challenge?
What term describes the specific, actionable lesson learned from analysing why an attempt failed?
What term describes trying a new approach specifically because a previous one didn't work, rather than giving up entirely?

res_l1_t3.technicalIntricacy: Resilience, extracting takeaways, and adapting one's approach are all connected skills for handling setbacks productively: bouncing back overall, learning something specific from what went wrong, and then actually changing behaviour based on that lesson.
res_l1_t3.realPurpose: Naming these skills precisely makes it easier to practice them deliberately after a setback, rather than only experiencing 'resilience' as a vague feeling.

variants.question: Is the thought 'This is hard right now, but I can improve with practice.' an example of growth-oriented or fixed-mindset self-talk?
distractors: Fixed-mindset self-talk
Neutral self-talk with no effect on motivation either way
Self-talk that only affects physical tasks, not mental ones

variants.question: Is the thought 'I'll never be able to do this, so there's no point trying.' an example of growth-oriented or fixed-mindset self-talk?
distractors: Growth-oriented self-talk
Neutral self-talk with no effect on motivation either way
Self-talk that only affects physical tasks, not mental ones

variants.question: Is the thought 'Let me figure out specifically what went wrong so I can adjust.' an example of growth-oriented or fixed-mindset self-talk?
distractors: Fixed-mindset self-talk
Neutral self-talk with no effect on motivation either way
Self-talk that only affects physical tasks, not mental ones

variants.question: Is the thought 'Only naturally talented people can succeed at this, and I'm clearly not one of them.' an example of growth-oriented or fixed-mindset self-talk?
distractors: Growth-oriented self-talk
Neutral self-talk with no effect on motivation either way
Self-talk that only affects physical tasks, not mental ones

res_l1_t4.technicalIntricacy: Growth-oriented self-talk frames a setback as a specific, improvable situation, while fixed-mindset self-talk frames it as a permanent, unchangeable limitation — and the internal language someone uses can meaningfully shape whether they keep trying or give up.
res_l1_t4.realPurpose: Noticing the difference between these two internal voices makes it possible to deliberately shift toward growth-oriented thinking during a difficult moment.

variants.question: What term describes a mix of long-term perseverance and passion for a goal that keeps someone working toward it despite setbacks?
What term describes a person's belief in their own ability to succeed at a specific task or challenge?
What term describes praise that focuses on someone's effort and strategy, rather than on fixed, innate talent?

res_l1_t5.technicalIntricacy: Grit describes sustained motivation over time, self-efficacy describes confidence in handling a specific challenge, and process praise reinforces effort and strategy rather than a fixed trait — three related but distinct ingredients that support resilience.
res_l1_t5.realPurpose: Knowing these terms precisely helps a student notice which ingredient of resilience they might be missing in a tough moment, rather than only feeling generally 'unmotivated.'

variants.question: Many well-known inventions, artworks and discoveries reached their final, successful form only after going through what?
variants.answer: Many earlier failed or imperfect versions and drafts
distractors: A single flawless first attempt, with no earlier versions at all
Pure luck, with no prior attempts, drafts or practice involved
A secret shortcut that skips the need for any practice or revision

variants.question: A student assumes that a finished, polished project must have been perfect from the very first attempt, with no earlier failed drafts along the way. What does this assumption overlook?
variants.answer: Most finished, polished work is actually the result of many earlier attempts, drafts and corrections that simply aren't visible in the final version
distractors: The assumption is correct — polished final work is almost always the result of a single perfect first attempt
Nothing is overlooked, since early drafts have no real effect on a final result
Only low-quality, unfinished projects ever involve multiple drafts or attempts

res_l1_t6.technicalIntricacy: The version of a project that eventually gets shown to the world is usually the last in a long, mostly invisible line of earlier drafts, prototypes and failed attempts, each of which contributed something toward the final result.
res_l1_t6.realPurpose: Knowing this helps a student expect (and accept) an imperfect first draft as a normal part of the process, rather than mistaking it for proof the whole project has failed.

variants.question: After a disappointing test result, a teacher simply tells a student 'do better next time' without explaining what to change. Is this specific or vague feedback?
distractors: Specific feedback
Neither specific nor vague — it counts as no feedback at all
Both specific and vague feedback at the same time

variants.question: After a disappointing test result, a teacher tells a student exactly which two topics they missed and suggests one practice strategy for each. Is this specific or vague feedback?
distractors: Vague feedback
Neither specific nor vague — it counts as no feedback at all
Both specific and vague feedback at the same time

res_l1_t7.technicalIntricacy: Specific feedback names the exact topic, step or habit to adjust, giving a clear starting point for the next attempt, while vague feedback only signals that something should change without saying what — making it much harder to actually act on.
res_l1_t7.realPurpose: Learning to ask for (or give) specific feedback turns a discouraging result into a concrete, usable plan for improvement.

variants.question: A student who isn't improving with one study method switches to a different method that suits how they learn, while still working toward the same overall goal. Is this quitting or a strategic pivot?
distractors: Quitting
Neither — this counts as abandoning the goal entirely
Both quitting and a strategic pivot at the same time

variants.question: A student gives up on a goal completely after a single setback, without ever adjusting their approach or trying an alternative method. Is this quitting or a strategic pivot?
distractors: A strategic pivot
Neither — this counts as improving the original approach
Both quitting and a strategic pivot at the same time

res_l1_t8.technicalIntricacy: A strategic pivot keeps the original goal in place while changing the method used to reach it, whereas quitting abandons the goal itself — the two can look similar in the moment (both involve stopping something), but they lead to very different outcomes.
res_l1_t8.realPurpose: Telling these two apart helps a student choose a genuinely more effective approach when one isn't working, instead of mistakenly treating every setback as a reason to give up entirely.

variants.question: Is struggling with a genuinely difficult, unfamiliar task a normal, expected part of learning, or proof that someone lacks the ability to ever succeed at it?
variants.answer: A normal, expected part of learning
distractors: Proof that someone lacks the ability to ever succeed at it
Proof that the task itself is impossible for anyone to learn
A sign that the person should switch to an entirely easier subject permanently

variants.question: A student assumes that if a new skill feels difficult at first, it must mean they simply aren't cut out for it. What is the flaw in this assumption?
variants.answer: Feeling difficulty with a new, unfamiliar skill is a normal early stage of learning it, not reliable evidence about long-term ability; most skills feel hard before they start to feel manageable with practice
distractors: The assumption is correct — a skill that feels hard at first will always continue to feel equally hard, no matter how much practice follows
Difficulty at the start of learning something new is extremely rare and usually signals a genuine lack of ability
There is no connection at all between early difficulty and how much practice a skill typically requires

res_l1_t9.technicalIntricacy: Early difficulty with a new skill mostly reflects unfamiliarity rather than a fixed ceiling on ability, since almost every skill requires an uncomfortable early stage before repeated practice makes it feel more natural.
res_l1_t9.realPurpose: Expecting some early struggle as normal helps a student stay with a new challenge long enough to actually improve, instead of quitting during the hardest and most temporary part of the learning curve.

variants.question: What term describes reaching out to a teacher, friend, or family member for guidance when stuck on a difficult challenge?
What term describes continuing to struggle with a problem completely alone, even when a hint or explanation from someone else could unblock progress much faster?

res_l1_t10.technicalIntricacy: Seeking support means recognising that continuing to struggle completely alone isn't the only (or always the best) option, and that asking for a hint, explanation or guidance can unblock progress far faster than repeated solo attempts.
res_l1_t10.realPurpose: Treating asking for help as a legitimate resilience strategy, rather than as a sign of weakness, makes students more likely to actually use it when they're genuinely stuck.

variants.question: A student practices a skill and improves their score by {{improvementPerSession}} points after each practice session. If they start with a score of {{startScore}}, what will their score be after {{sessions}} practice sessions?
distractors: {{distractorA}}
